title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pairs = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, execution accounting, the preregistered Mininet 10% holdout (20 tasks) that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational gains but risks producing incorrect or unsafe network changes that can violate policies or cause outages. Prior work proposes grounding and verification—combine generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR)—to catch and correct unsafe candidates before application. However, the practical marginal value of automated repair depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator and sampling policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question and a sealed analysis plan to isolate the marginal effect of deterministic GVR when the generator output is held fixed across conditions. Research question: Does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? Our contributions are (1) a preregistered paired confirmatory design that enforces shared initial generation to isolate the validator/repair effect; (2) a complete audited execution on 200 machine‑checkable tasks with deterministic accounting; and (3) an artifact‑grounded interpretation explaining why the preregistered reduction hypothesis was not evaluable on this workload, together with operational recommendations for future evaluations.
sections.related_work: Surveys and empirical studies document LLM factual errors, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism, and propose mitigation patterns including retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, and guarded agent architectures. Prototype systems show feasibility for intent→configuration generation but often lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate studies. Architectural proposals therefore recommend integrating LLM generation with deterministic validators (Batfish‑style or domain‑specific checkers) and with controlled guardrails; red‑team audits document configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can change safety outcomes. This study situates itself as an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal benefit of a deterministic validator+repair applied to a fixed generator output—complementary to prior prototype and red‑team work that typically explores unconditional or adversarial sampling strategies.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration. We preregistered a paired confirmatory plan (study id cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixing n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs were computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power was planned under an assumed baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and a targeted 50% relative reduction; these assumptions justified sample size but did not determine analysis after execution.

Task bank and validators. The task bank contained 200 machine‑checkable intent→configuration examples spanning four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge). Each task encodes initial and expected final states plus workflow policies (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group minima). The primary deterministic checker enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and produces structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to reveal validator blind spots; the holdout produced zero disagreements in this run. The preregistration, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle for audit.

Shared‑initial adapter semantics and determinism reconciliation. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced a shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single initial candidate which was reused by both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (validator+repair) conditions. This isolates the marginal effect of validation+repair on an identical generator output. The runtime artifacts show that the adapter‑enforced single shared invocation occurred for all tasks (provider audit fields record 200 hosted model call events and a stage count corresponding to shared_initial_generation). Notably, the model configuration metadata lists "temperature": null; determinism in this run was therefore achieved by adapter enforcement of the shared_initial policy and audited provider accounting rather than by an explicit labeled temperature parameter within the model configuration file. The specific artifacts that demonstrate adapter enforcement and accounting are present in the archived execution bundle (see the archived execution manifest and the deterministic reconciliation artifacts) and were used to reconcile the runtime determinism semantics.

Repair policy, budgeting, and handling. If the primary validator reported violations the preregistered policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM; any repaired candidate was re‑validated. The adapter enforced an absolute model‑call cap (initial + repairs ≤ 400). Missingness rules deterministically excluded pairs where both conditions failed due to infrastructure execution errors; tasks flagged for validator–emulator disagreement were to be excluded from the primary analysis per the preregistered contamination plan, with deterministic sensitivity analyses planned for alternative treatments. We document one reproducibility gap here: the explicit randomized selection seed that determined which tasks comprised the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive, which prevents deterministic bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the exact holdout draw despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements. This gap is treated explicitly as a limitation below.

Statistical implementation. The confirmatory test used an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the 2×2 paired table (n11, n10, n01, n00) produced by the paired design. Bootstrap percentile CIs used 10,000 resamples with the preregistered seed. Secondary exploratory analyses (logistic regressions, repair‑iteration summaries) were preplanned but conditional on repair events occurring.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run completed all planned episodes. Completed pairs = 200 (one shared initial generation per pair), model calls used = 200, repair calls used = 0, maximum model calls allowed = 400. Provider/adaptor audit records confirm a single shared initial invocation per task across both conditions.

Primary outcomes. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. Paired contingency table: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and inferential test the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0%.

Repair and secondary outcomes. No validator failures occurred and the preregistered repair branch was never invoked; consequently, planned secondary estimands (repair iterations per repaired task, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) are empty for this run.

Contamination check. The preregistered Mininet holdout (randomized 10% sample, 20 tasks) produced zero validator–emulator disagreement flags in the executed holdout sample. As noted in Methods, the explicit labeled seed selecting the holdout is absent from the artifact labels, which prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the selected holdout despite the reported zero disagreements.

Representative diagnostics. Archived validator traces for representative tasks show parsed_command_count matching required_command_count and validation_after.valid = true, demonstrating the task bank included nontrivial dependency patterns (difficulty labels of "medium", "hard", and "very_hard") even though generator outputs satisfied the machine‑checkable constraints under the chosen generation policy.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The null outcome (zero baseline validator failures) is an artifact‑grounded empirical result: on this curated task bank and under the frozen shared_initial generation policy the LLM outputs satisfied the deterministic validator for every task, so there was no validator‑detectable failure margin for GVR to reduce. That outcome does not imply GVR is generally unnecessary; it means that the marginal utility of automated repair is workload‑ and generator‑policy dependent.

Why the degenerate result occurred. Archived per‑task traces show generator outputs aligned with explicitly required_sequences and workflow constraints; parsed_command_count equaled required_command_count and violation_count = 0. The shared_initial paired design intentionally removed sampling variance—alternative designs that allow independent multi‑sample draws per condition or nonzero temperature could increase observed baseline failure prevalence and expose repair opportunities. Additionally, the held validator passed the 10% Mininet emulator holdout in this run, but the absence of the labeled holdout selection seed limits the exact reproducibility of that corroboration.

Methodological tradeoffs and operational implications. The shared_initial paired design provides a clean causal contrast of validator+repair applied to a fixed generator output; it intentionally excludes repair benefits that rely on re‑sampling or stochastic candidate diversity. For operational assurance, practitioners should (1) measure unconditional failure prevalence under their intended generation policy (multi‑sample, per‑condition draws), (2) expand validator fidelity and emulator coverage to reduce oracle blind spots, and (3) consider larger or multi‑step repair budgets or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation when baseline failures are nontrivial. Where baseline failures are rare under the production generation policy, resources invested in broader validator coverage and adversarial testing may yield greater safety returns than a narrow single‑attempt repair loop.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration and audited adapter enforcement; analysis accounting is deterministic. Construct validity depends on validator expressiveness—deterministic checkers codify a finite set of constraints and can omit device idiosyncrasies. External validity is limited by a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), the shared_initial deterministic sampling policy, and a curated synthetic/public task bank. Conclusion validity is constrained by the degenerate paired table (no discordant pairs) so the preregistered effect estimate and inferential test are uninformative about potential reductions in nonzero baseline regimes.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired confirmatory study comparing LLM‑only generation and a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 intent→configuration NetOps tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic intent/constraint checker. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding a paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis was not evaluable because baseline validator‑detected failures were absent. This artifact‑grounded outcome clarifies that GVR’s marginal value depends on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage; future confirmatory work should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failures, increase sampling diversity, expand validation fidelity via larger emulation or device tests, and permit larger repair budgets or human escalation to characterize practical operational gains.

limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
